'''George Szekeres''' ({{IPA|hu|ˈsɛkɛrɛʃ|lang}}; 29 May 1911 – 28 August 2005), born '''Szekeres György''', was a Hungarian–Australian mathematician. After migrating to Australia after World War II, he worked first for the [[University of Adelaide]], and then  the [[University of New South Wales]]. He is known for his co-authoring a paper with fellow Hungarian mathematician [[Paul Erdős]] known as the "[[Happy Ending problem]]", and married mathematician [[Esther Klein]].

==Early years and education==
Szekeres György was born in [[Budapest]], [[Kingdom of Hungary|Hungary]], on 29 May 1911.<ref name=smh_obituary/><ref name="mac">{{cite web | title=George Szekeres |first1=J J|last1= O'Connor |first2= E F |last2= Robertson| author2-link=E F Robertson | website=[[MacTutor History of Mathematics archive|MacTutor]] | date=March 2006 | url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Szekeres/ | access-date=10 March 2026}} Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International License.</ref>

He received his degree in [[chemistry]] at the [[Royal Joseph University]] (later Technical University of Budapest).{{efn|University name per ADB entry on [[George Svéd]], and corroborated in the article about the university.<ref name=howell>{{cite web | last=Howell | first=P. A. | title=George Svéd | website=[[Australian Dictionary of Biography]] | date=6 March 2020 | url=https://adb.anu.edu.au/biography/sved-george-29799 | access-date=7 March 2026| quote =This article was published: in the Australian Dictionary of Biography, Volume 19, 2021; online in 2020}}</ref>}}<ref name=smh_obituary/> He graduated with a degree in [[chemical engineering]] in 1933, having studied only one mathematical course, in [[calculus]].<ref name=mac/>

The so-called "[[Happy Ending problem]]" is an example of how mathematics pervaded Szekeres's life.<ref name=peterson2000/> During 1933, George and several other students met frequently, often at the ''[[Anonymous (statue)|Anonymous]]'' statue in [[City Park (Budapest)|City Park]],<ref name=universe/> to discuss mathematics. At one of these meetings, [[Esther Klein]] proposed the problem:<ref name=peterson2000/> "Given five points in the plane in [[general position]], prove that four of them form a [[Convex polygon|convex]] [[quadrilateral]]." After allowing George, [[Paul Erdős]], and the other students to scratch their heads for some time, Esther explained her proof.<ref name=peterson2000>{{cite web |url=http://www.maa.org/mathland/mathtrek_10_3_00.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20010121105100/http://www.maa.org/mathland/mathtrek_10_3_00.html |date= 2 October 2000| archive-date=21 January 2001 |title=Ivars Peterson's MathTrek -Planes of Budapest |first= Ivars| last= Peterson}}</ref>  Subsequently, George and Paul wrote a paper (1935) that generalises this result;<ref>{{cite journal  | author = Erdős, Paul  | author-link = Paul Erdős  | author2 = Szekeres, George  | title = A combinatorial problem in geometry  | journal = Compositio Mathematica  | volume = 2  | pages = 463–470 | year = 1935 | url = https://www.numdam.org/item?id=CM_1935__2__463_0}}</ref> it is regarded as one of the foundational works in the field of [[combinatorial geometry]].{{citation needed|date=March 2026}} Erdős dubbed the original problem the "Happy Ending" problem because it resulted in the marriage of George and Esther.<ref name=universe/>

==Career==
Szekeres worked for six years in Budapest as an [[analytical chemist]], and during this time married [[Esther Szekeres|Esther Klein]] in 1937. Being [[Jewish]], the family had to escape from the [[Nazism|Nazi]] persecution so Szekeres took a job as a leather chemist in [[Shanghai]], China. There they lived through World War II, the Japanese occupation and the beginnings of the Communist revolution.<ref name=smh_obituary>{{cite web | title=Obituary: A world of teaching and numbers | website=The Sydney Morning Herald | date=7 November 2005 | url=https://www.smh.com.au/national/a-world-of-teaching-and-numbers-times-two-20051107-gdme4e.html | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251116085236/https://www.smh.com.au/national/a-world-of-teaching-and-numbers-times-two-20051107-gdme4e.html | archive-date=16 November 2025 | url-status=live | access-date=7 March 2026}}</ref><ref name=mac/>

In 1948, Szekeres was offered and accepted a position as lecturer at the [[University of Adelaide]], Australia,<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=George Szekeres - Biography |url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Szekeres/ |access-date=2025-05-23 |website=Maths History |language=en}}</ref> and the family (with their son, born in China), moving to [[Adelaide]], [[South Australia]], in June 1948. Esther also taught at the university.<ref name=mac/>

In 1964, the family moved to [[Sydney]], where Szekeres took a position as professor of mathematics at the [[University of New South Wales]] (UNSW), and taught there until his retirement in 1976, when he became emeritus professor. He continued to publish papers after his retirement.<ref name=mac/><ref name=":0" />

In 1978 he published a joint paper with Erdős entitled "Some number theoretic problems on [[binomial coefficients]]". His 1985 paper "Distribution of labelled trees by diameter" analysed the graphs described by the title and, among many other results, found the expected value of the diameter of a random labelled tree on ''nn'' vertices.<ref name=mac/>  Also in 1985 he showed his continuing interest in using computers in mathematical investigations with "Computer examination of the two-dimensional simultaneous approximation constant".<ref name=mac/>

He worked closely with many prominent mathematicians throughout his life, including Erdős, his wife Esther, [[Pál Turán]], [[Béla Bollobás]], [[Ronald Graham]], [[Alf van der Poorten]], [[Miklós Laczkovich]], and [[John Coates (mathematician)|John Coates]].{{citation needed|date=March 2026}} He worked on many problems and published many papers, especially in the field of [[combinatorics]], [[graph theory]] in particular.<ref name=mac/> Many mathematical concepts bear his name, including [[Szekeres snark]], [[Kruskal–Szekeres coordinates]], [[Szekeres–Wilf number]], and the [[Erdős–Szekeres theorem]].

==Other activities==
Szekeres was a founder member of the [[Australian Mathematical Society]] in August 1956, and served as its president from 1972 to 1974.<ref name=mac/>

He devised problems for secondary school [[mathematical olympiad]]s ran by UNSW, and for a yearly undergraduate competition ran by the [[Sydney University]] Mathematics Society.{{citation needed|date=March 2026}}

==Recognition and honours==
* ?: Elected to the [[Hungarian Academy of Sciences]]<ref name=mac/>
* 1963: Elected to the [[Australian Academy of Science]]<ref name=mac/>
* 1968: [[Thomas Ranken Lyle Medal]] of the [[Australian Academy of Science]]<ref name=mac/> 
* May 2001:  [[festschrift]] held at UNSW in honour of his ninetieth birthday{{citation needed|date=March 2026}} 
* 2001: [[Australian Centenary Medal]], "for service to Australian society and science in pure mathematics"<ref name=CM>{{cite web |title= Centenary Medal |url= https://honours.pmc.gov.au/honours/awards/1127630 |work= It's an Honour |publisher=Honours and Awards Branch, Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet|access-date=20 June 2010 |location=Canberra |date=1 January 2001}}</ref>
* 2001: Establishment of the [[George Szekeres Medal]] by the [[Australian Mathematical Society]]{{citation needed|date=March 2026}}  
* 2002: [[Member of the Order of Australia]] (AM), "for service to mathematics and science, particularly as a contributor to education and research, to the support and development of the University of New South Wales Mathematics Competition and the [[Australian Mathematical Olympiad]] Team"<ref name=AM>{{cite web |title= Member of the Order of Australia |work= It's an Honour |url=https://honours.pmc.gov.au/honours/awards/1040563 |publisher=Honours and Awards Branch, Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet |access-date=20 June 2010 |location=Canberra |date=10 June 2002}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Szkeres married Esther Klein on 13 June 1937.<ref name=mac/>

When they first moved to Australia after the war, the Szekeres shared an apartment in [[Adelaide]] with mathematician [[Márta Svéd]], an old school friend of Esther, and her husband [[George Svéd]], for three years. Esther and George had two children.<ref name=smh_obituary/><ref name=universe>{{cite book| title=A Universe of Sufficient Size| first= Miriam|last= Sved| chapter=Acknowledgements| pages= 312–313|ISBN= 9781743535127|date=2019 }}</ref> After moving to Sydney, they bought a house in [[Turramurra]], which they had obtained at a low price owing to it having belonged to a person who had died in suspicious circumstances in the [[Bogle–Chandler case]].<ref name=mac/>

Szekeres loved art and music, particularly [[chamber music]]. He was an accomplished musician, playing [[violin]] and [[viola]]. He played in the North Sydney Symphony Orchestra and the [[Ku-ring-gai Philharmonic Orchestra]], and was founding treasurer of the latter until 2000. He also loved walking and even in his 80s enjoyed long walks with his daughter Judith.<ref name=mac/>

After returning to Adelaide in 2004, George and Esther died within an hour of each other on 28 August 2005<ref name=smh_obituary/><ref name=universe/> in Wynwood Nursing Home<ref name=mac/> in [[Norwood, South Australia|Norwood]] (now closed).<ref>{{cite web | title=Wynwood Nursing Home (Closed) | website=Aged Care Quality and Safety Commission | date=7 October 2022 | url=https://www.agedcarequality.gov.au/services/wynwood-nursing-home-closed | access-date=10 March 2026}}</ref>

===In fiction===
The Svéds' granddaughter, author [[Miriam Sved]],<ref>{{cite web| url=https://historicalnovelsociety.org/reviews/a-universe-of-sufficient-size/| website= Historical Novel Society| title=A Universe of Sufficient Size, Written by Miriam Sved| first =Georgia Rose| last= Phillips|quote= Appeared in: ''HNR'' Issue 90 (November 2019) | date= November 2019| access-date=9 March 2026}}</ref><ref name=hardy>{{cite web | last=Hardy | first=Karen | title=Miriam Sved: Game Day novel on the ball | website=The Sydney Morning Herald | date=14 August 2014 | url=https://www.smh.com.au/entertainment/books/miriam-sved-game-day-novel-on-the-ball-20140814-103x8y.html | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240804212857/https://www.smh.com.au/entertainment/books/miriam-sved-game-day-novel-on-the-ball-20140814-103x8y.html | archive-date=4 August 2024 | url-status=live | access-date=9 March 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | last=Sved | first=Miriam | title=fiction | website=[[Overland (magazine)]] | date=15 April 2013 | url=https://overland.org.au/previous-issues/issue-198/fiction-miriam-sved/ | access-date=9 March 2026}}</ref> wrote the historical novel ''A Universe of Sufficient Size'', published in 2019.<ref>{{cite web | title= Miriam Sved | website=Miriam Sved – Author | url=https://miriamsved.com.au/about/ | access-date=9 March 2026}}</ref> It tells the story of a group of Jewish mathematicians in Hungary who flee the country, which she based on stories she had heard from Márta Svéd. While the story is fictional, several characters are loosely based on people in Svéd's circle, in particular Esther and George Szekeres, as well as Paul Erdős.<ref name=universe/>
